clue.text: Author upsets W. B. for example, twice or three times

indicators.note: upsets says the gathered letters are knocked over and rearranged into a new order

parts.note: the initials W and B taken as written

indicators.note: twice tells us the abbreviation for 'for example' is used two times over

parts.note: for example is abbreviated EG
the little word or written out three times in a row

explanation.surface: Someone keeps knocking over the poet W. B. Yeats, more than once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'W. B. for example' looks like a reference to Yeats, but it is just raw letters: W, B, EG twice and OR three times, all shuffled ('upsets') into the name of the Victorian travel writer of Lavengro.
explanation.definitionFit: George Borrow was a nineteenth-century English writer known for Lavengro and The Romany Rye.

clue.text: Annoy soldier perhaps, like Captain Oates

parts.note: to annoy or irritate someone is to gall them
a soldier ant is one kind of ant, so ant is an example

explanation.surface: Irritating a soldier, in the manner of the Antarctic explorer Oates.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Oates walked out into the Antarctic blizzard to save his companions on Scott's expedition, the model of brave self-sacrifice.
explanation.definitionFit: Oates's famous self-sacrifice on the polar expedition is the classic example of a brave, chivalrous act.

clue.text: Rumour I don't put out

indicators.note: put out suggests the letters are disturbed and set into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to spread a rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' rearranges the letters of I DONT; the result is a French phrase used in English, literally 'it is said'.
explanation.definitionFit: An on dit is a piece of gossip, something people are saying.

clue.text: Country like England ? Less pleasant

indicators.note: less here means without, so the words and pleasant are dropped from the famous phrase

parts.note: Blake's hymn Jerusalem calls England a green and pleasant land

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that a country resembles England, only nastier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less' reads as a comparative ('less pleasant' = nastier) but means 'minus'. Blake's line 'England's green and pleasant land', from the hymn Jerusalem, loses 'and pleasant'.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenland is the large Arctic island territory belonging to Denmark.

clue.text: Complain it's like Yeats's glade, in short

indicators.note: in short asks for the abbreviation, so the word loud is cut down to its musical symbol

parts.note: Yeats's poem The Lake Isle of Innisfree speaks of the bee-loud glade

explanation.surface: A remark that something resembles the glade in a Yeats poem, briefly put.
explanation.walkthrough: In music F (forte) means loud, so bee-loud abbreviated becomes BEE + F.
explanation.definitionFit: To beef is slang for to grumble or moan about something.

clue.text: Logical and right to replace leader of race

indicators.note: to replace tells us one letter is swapped out for another
leader of points to the opening letter of the race's name as the one taken out

parts.note: the Grand National is Britain's most famous horse race

explanation.surface: A sensible plan to put someone in place of the head of a racing team.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National, the famous British steeplechase, is often just called the National; its N is swapped for R.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rational is reasoned and sensible, following logic.

clue.text: But as a newspaper it wouldn't be stopped

definitions.text: But as a newspaper it wouldn't be stopped

parts.words: But as a newspaper it wouldn't be stopped
parts.note: the musical instrument has stops; the same word meaning a newspaper or official mouthpiece has none, and nobody would stop the presses

explanation.surface: A newspaper that must keep running whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a pipe instrument, worked by stops, and a newspaper or journal speaking for a party, which has no stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A party's newspaper is called its mouthpiece or house journal, the same word as the stop-pulling church instrument.

clue.text: Post-Christian writer

parts.note: the fairy-tale author Hans Christian had a surname coming straight after Christian

explanation.surface: An author for an age after religion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post-Christian' looks like theology but means literally 'after Christian', in the Danish storyteller's full name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hans Christian Andersen was the Danish author of fairy tales such as The Little Mermaid.

clue.text: What in the world is under the crust?

definitions.text: What in the world is under the crust?

parts.words: What in the world is under the crust?
parts.note: sounds like a puzzled question about a pie, but asks literally about the layer of the Earth below its crust

explanation.surface: A baffled diner asks what is inside the pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What in the world' sounds like an exclamation, but means 'in the Earth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Geologists name the thick rocky layer between the Earth's crust and core this way.

clue.text: Deposit by eg freemasons before end of account

parts.note: freemasons meet in lodges, so they are lodge men

indicators.note: end of picks out the final letter of the word account

explanation.surface: Freemasons pay money in before the account closes.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodgement is something lodged, such as money deposited or sediment laid down.

clue.text: Sail Columbus raised here

definitions.meaning: a large jib sail on a yacht
the Italian port where the explorer grew up

explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' looks like raising a sail but means brought up as a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A genoa is a big foresail on a racing yacht, and the Italian seaport was Christopher Columbus's birthplace.

clue.text: In any century a tragic hero appears

indicators.note: In tells us one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a century is a hundred, and ton is slang for a hundred

explanation.surface: In every age a doomed hero turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts TON (a hundred, a century) inside ANY.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony is the doomed lover in Shakespeare's tragedy with Cleopatra.

clue.text: Sends out broadcast that's most fit — for radio ?

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so these letters are spread out and rearranged

explanation.surface: A station transmits the healthiest programme, suited to radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges SENDS OUT. 'for radio?' is a joke: sound is what radio broadcasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound means healthy and in good condition, so the superlative means healthiest.

clue.text: Dickensian chap born under Aries?

definitions.note: used as a noun here, a character from Dickens

indicators.note: born under places the second piece beneath the first, so the man comes after the ram

parts.note: Aries is the ram of the zodiac, and a tup is a ram
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A Dickens character with a zodiac sign of the ram.
explanation.walkthrough: Tracy Tupman is one of the Pickwick Club in The Pickwick Papers. 'born under' places MAN after TUP, a dialect word for a ram (Aries).
explanation.definitionFit: Tracy Tupman is the romantic member of the Pickwick Club in Dickens's first novel.

clue.text: Archer going to' shoot

parts.note: an ancient horse archer who loosed arrows while riding away, giving the phrase for a parting shot

explanation.surface: A bowman about to fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Mounted archers of ancient Parthia fired backwards while retreating; 'going' hints at leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: Parthian horsemen were famed for firing arrows while in retreat.

clue.text: Liberal behaviour or start of Socialism, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the spoken sound gives the answer, not the spelling

parts.note: Socialism starts with a capital, that is a large S

explanation.surface: A choice between generosity and the first stirrings of socialist politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start of Socialism' is the capital letter, a 'large S', which said quickly sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Largesse is generous giving, freely handing out money or gifts.

clue.text: Land once in Africa, or beach

definitions.meaning: the former British colony now called Ghana
a golden shoreline, taken as a seaside strip

explanation.definitionFit: The Gold Coast was the colonial name of Ghana, and a golden stretch of sand by the sea is a beach.

clue.text: People ducking unfortunate king up at Oxford?

indicators.note: ducking means plunging into water, so one piece goes into the river

parts.note: the Thames at Oxford is called the Isis

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Shakespeare's King Lear is the most unfortunate of kings

explanation.surface: Locals dunking an unlucky king who has come to Oxford university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns LEAR into RAEL, and 'ducking' plunges it into ISIS, the Thames at Oxford; 'up at Oxford' also suggests being a student there.
explanation.definitionFit: Israelis are the people of the state of Israel.

clue.text: Sad pair evicted initially, going wrong here

indicators.note: going wrong suggests the letters are scrambled out of their proper order
initially takes just the opening letter of the word evicted

explanation.surface: A miserable couple thrown out of their home, where things went awry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going wrong' rearranges SAD PAIR plus E. The sad pair are Adam and Eve, evicted from the Garden of Eden after things went wrong there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garden of Eden, from which Adam and Eve were cast out, is the earthly paradise.

clue.text: Specify one penny for his turnover

definitions.text: Specify one penny for his turnover

indicators.note: turnover means the whole string is turned over, read from the far end back

parts.note: to specify is to name
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Naming a price of one penny for a pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turnover' reverses NAME + I + P; a turnover is also a folded pastry, the very thing this street seller would price at a penny, as in Simple Simon.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie-seller would sell turnovers, folded fruit or meat pastries, at a fixed price.

clue.text: Fine shot, but short-sighted?

definitions.meaning: in cricket a ... is a deft stroke deflecting the ball fine behind the wicket
read literally as seen only briefly, a quick look

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, 'fine' means close to the line of the wicket behind the batsman. 'short-sighted' means not myopic but 'seen for a short time'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket stroke angled fine off the bat, and a quick brief look, share the word.

clue.text: Blow up, so destroying most of 3'

indicators.note: destroying says the letters are broken up and put back together differently
most of means nearly all of the word is used, with its tail dropped

parts.note: 3 refers to the answer to clue 3 down, the Arctic island country

explanation.surface: Blowing up a country, wrecking most of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims the answer to 3 down to GREENLA, and 'destroying' rearranges those seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To blow up a photograph is to make it bigger.

clue.text: Light in this place, and others outside

indicators.note: outside says the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: et al is the Latin abbreviation for and others
in this place means here

explanation.surface: A lamp is here, and other lamps are out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts ET AL, Latin for 'and others', around HERE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal means airy and delicate, light as air.

clue.text: Managed many head of Hereford here, perhaps

definitions.text: Managed many head of Hereford here, perhaps

parts.note: to manage a business is to run it, past tense ran
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, standing for many

indicators.note: head of takes just the opening letter of Hereford

explanation.surface: A large herd of Hereford cattle was looked after here.
explanation.walkthrough: Hereford is a breed of beef cattle; 'head' looks like heads of cattle but takes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cattle farm is where large herds of beef cattle are run.

clue.text: Bad hand makes South advance slowly

parts.note: to crawl is to move forward slowly

explanation.surface: A poor hand at cards lets the South player progress only gradually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hand' suggests cards, with South a bridge player, but it means handwriting.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand here means handwriting, and a scrawl is untidy, illegible writing.

clue.text: Creature that will increase but not multiply?

definitions.meaning: a snake, the venomous viper of Britain

definitions.text: that will increase but not multiply?
definitions.meaning: one who makes things greater by summing, not by times tables

explanation.walkthrough: The joke plays on creatures that multiply (breed), and the snake that can only add.
explanation.definitionFit: The adder is Britain's native venomous snake, and literally one who adds sums.

clue.text: This king is showing off what's nicked for the Crown

definitions.text: This king is showing off what's nicked for the Crown

parts.words: This king is showing off what's nicked for the Crown
parts.note: the bird's name followed by king makes a word for showing off, and the royal birds on the Thames are marked by nicks on the beak

explanation.surface: A monarch flaunts what has been stolen for the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nicked' suggests stolen, but in the old custom of swan upping on the Thames birds were marked by nicks on the beak; unmarked birds belong to the Crown.
explanation.definitionFit: Mute swans on open water in Britain have traditionally been treated as royal property.

clue.text: A drink that includes a repeat order

indicators.note: that includes says the drink holds the second piece inside it

parts.note: gin is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone orders a drink and then calls for the same again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that includes' puts A inside GIN, after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: An encore or call for a repeat is the command to do it once more.

clue.text: Scot's illegal punch

definitions.meaning: Scot is, a person from Scotland's southern part
a blow landed below the belt, a low one that lands

explanation.walkthrough: In boxing a punch below the belt is illegal, so a 'low lander' is a foul blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scot from the southern lowlands is so called, and a foul boxing blow is one landed low.

clue.text: At work, Smith understood this source of old stories

definitions.meaning: Longfellow's village blacksmith works beneath a spreading tree, so he stood under it
a stale, often-told joke is called a chestnut

explanation.walkthrough: 'understood' is read as 'stood under': 'Under a spreading chestnut tree the village smithy stands', from Longfellow's The Village Blacksmith.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's blacksmith worked beneath this tree, and stale old jokes are called by the name of its nuts.
